newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Kenwood defends tactics, strategy.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Kenwood defends tactics, strategy.

text.p: British-based electrical appliance maker Kenwood Appliances Plc said on Tuesday it stood by what it called an active plan for rebuilding profitability as it faces pressure from rebel shareholders to consider a sale or merger.

Chief executive Tim Beech told Reuters in a phone interview after the company announced its half-year results that it was unreasonable of rebel shareholder UK Active Value, which built up a 9.0 percent stake following a company profit warning in July, to target Kenwood's management team as most were new. And, while he understood that he faced pressure as the senior member of the management team, he defended his tactics.

"Some of the guns have been focused in on me. Clearly, the actions being taken are very sensible and clearly they are exactly the same actions that would have been taken by anybody else," Beech said, in reference to the profit improvement plan.

He also said the company was emphasising that a weakening in its results for the six months to October 4, when pretax profits fell to 3.29 million stg from 7.40 million a year ago, was due to a phase of serious market weakness and one-off factors.
"I don't control the consumers in Italy and France (where demand for small appliances has plunged), or the weather, which was the main issue for our air conditioning," Beech said.

Describing the line of attack taken by UK Active Value (UKAV), which is led by Julian Treger and Brian Myerson, Beech said it seemed the rebels preferred to agitate for change via the news media rather than talking to the company.

Kenwood today denied reports its smaller rival Pifco Plc had made an offer from the firm, and Beech ruled out any serious consideration of Pifco as a partner, saying he felt serious analysis of its performance would show it to have poorer underlying profitability and product positioning.
"Last year our return on capital employed was 34 percent, while Pifco's was more like 14 or 15 percent," he said.

Although the whole market had weakened, in Italy in particular, since last Christmas the company had gained market share. It was the market leader for kitchen appliances in the United Kingdom with 49 percent, he added.

As well as seeking manufacturing efficiencies, the programme of profit restoration would also centre on hopes for a large number of new products coming in later this year, the results of which should start feeding in next year, Beech said.
The cost implications of these moves were already taken in the exisiting operating costs, he added, saying the company had invested a lot in research and development.
